title: Choose a representation that exposes the relationship
chapter: Read the question into a useful model
goal: Choose a line, table, sketch or equation that reveals the relationship.

scenes.visual: One line of information resolves into four small models: a line, a table, a sketch and an equation. Each reveals a different relationship.
scenes.narration: A difficult-looking question can become much clearer as soon as you draw the right picture. A line shows order. A table sets comparisons side by side. A sketch makes shapes and boundaries visible. An equation holds a relationship in place. Choose the one that helps you see what the question is asking.

scenes.visual: Draw one fence panel with a post at either end, then attach another panel to show the shared post. Trace intervals and points in two colours.
scenes.narration: Picture a fence. Your eye can follow every post or every panel between two posts. A sketch gives both counts a place on the same line. The words each end tell us where the fence starts and stops. Mark those ends first. Then look for what repeats between them.

scenes.visual: Establish a straight 30 m fence, mark seven equally spaced positions from 0 to 30 and hold the complete problem before counting.
scenes.narration: A straight fence is thirty metres long. There is a post at each end, and the posts are five metres apart. How many posts are there? Draw the full thirty metres. Mark the left end as zero, and mark off spaces of five metres.

scenes.visual: Six gaps light up and hand their count to the post at each right-hand end. Reveal the starting post separately. Build the equalities one at a time.
scenes.narration: Thirty metres divided into five-metre spaces gives six gaps. Follow each gap to its right-hand end. That accounts for six posts. The post at zero sits before the first gap, so add it once. Six gaps, plus that starting post, makes seven posts.

scenes.visual: The six panels fold into a regular hexagonal loop. The end markers meet, then the map from each gap to its right-hand post is visible around the loop.
scenes.narration: Now join the ends to make a closed fence, using the same six equal panels. Watch the last post come back to the very first one. They meet at a single corner. Each panel now ends at a different post, and all posts are included. That makes six gaps and six posts.

scenes.visual: Place Sam on a line of figures. Build ranks from both ends, then colour the eight people in front and five behind and count Sam once.
scenes.narration: Try the same kind of line with a queue. Sam is ninth from the front and sixth from the back. How many people are there? Eight stand in front of Sam, and five stand behind. Eight, plus Sam, plus five, makes fourteen. Both ranks include Sam, so give Sam one place in the picture.

scenes.visual: Build a table with pencil counts, prices in dollars and a computed price per pencil. Align the comparison for the two boxes.
scenes.narration: A table helps when there are several things to compare. Box A contains eight pencils and costs sixteen dollars. Box B contains four pencils and costs twelve dollars. Add a price per pencil column. The divisions give two dollars and three dollars. Box A costs more for the box and less for each pencil.

scenes.visual: Slide two labelled four-by-three mats along their short sides. Reveal the two coincident interior edges. Trace the outside and build 14 + 14 − 3 − 3 = 22 metres.
scenes.narration: A sketch reveals a boundary. Join two mats, each four metres by three metres, along their three-metre sides. How much edge is exposed? Each mat has fourteen metres around it. The pair has twenty-eight before joining. The shared edge removes three metres from each mat, so the equation gives twenty-two metres outside.

scenes.visual: Return to the four models. End on the notebook question and a line with just its endpoints so the learner can draw their own model.
scenes.narration: Choose a line for order and gaps, a table for comparisons, and a sketch for shape and boundaries. Use an equation to show how the quantities fit together. Your turn. Trees are planted every four metres along a forty-metre path, including both ends. How many trees are there? Sketch it first.

notebook_exercise: Trees are planted every 4 m along a 40 m path, including both ends. How many trees are there?
notebook_answer: 40 ÷ 4 = 10 gaps. The starting tree plus one at the end of each gap makes 11 trees.
